title: The Word was made flesh (CCC 456–460)
hookLine: God became human to save us, show us love, and share his life

cards: Sunday Mass. The whole church is standing, saying the Creed together, words that are easy to say on autopilot. Then, midway, something strange happens.
At one line, heads go down. People bow. On Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation, they do more: they drop to one knee, right there in the pew, mid-sentence.
Kids who don't know why do it because the grown-ups do. The line is about God doing something no one expected. Today: the Word made flesh.

teach.b: The line is this: and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man. First, the word. Incarnate comes from the Latin caro, carnis: flesh, the same root as carnivore and chili con carne.

Incarnation means, bluntly, God in meat and bone. John's Gospel says it in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." The Word is the eternal Son, who was with God and was God, and he took flesh.
Second, why. The Catechism gives four reasons, worth counting on your fingers.
One: to save us, by reconciling us with God.

teach.h: THAT WE MIGHT SHARE GOD'S LIFE.
teach.b: Two: so that we might know God's love, which John says was shown by God sending his Son. Three: to be our model of holiness, a life you can actually watch.
Four: to make us, in the words of Second Peter, partakers of the divine nature. Third, that last one surprises people.
The Catechism quotes Athanasius, a bishop of Alexandria, who put it in one bold line: the Son of God became man so that we might become God. Theologians call it divinization.
It doesn't mean people stop being creatures; it means God's life can be given to them. Fourth, the name.
Matthew's Gospel calls the child Emmanuel, "which being interpreted is, God with us."

teach.h: AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.
teach.b: Not God above, looking down. God with skin, who got hungry, tired, and thirsty. That's why heads bow in the Creed: it's the moment Catholics remember that the distance between God and people was crossed from God's side.

how: At Sunday Mass, Catholics bow during the Creed at the words about the Incarnation, and on Christmas and the Annunciation they genuflect at those words instead.

o: a holy man raised up to become God
God appearing to look human, like a vision
God the Son taking on real human flesh

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: God became man so we might become God

s: the Catechism gives only one reason for the Incarnation
it gives four: to save us, to show God's love, to be our model, and to share God's life.
incarnate shares a root with carnivore
both come from the Latin caro, carnis: flesh.
sharing God's life means people stop being creatures
Catholics say God's life is given to us while we remain creatures.

games.q: it's Christmas morning Mass. the Creed reaches and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary. what does the congregation do?
o: genuflect, going down on one knee.
games.why: on Christmas and the Annunciation Catholics genuflect at these words; on other Sundays they bow.

practice: If you know the Creed, say it slowly to yourself, and at was incarnate, bow your head, or, if you're able and it feels right, go down on one knee, the way the Church does at Christmas; if you don't, just say the six words: and the Word was made flesh.
Then stay there and notice your own flesh, your hands, your breath, the weight of your body: what Catholics say God took on.

wordCard.voice: Incarnation. From the Latin for flesh: the Son of God taking a real human body and soul, to save us, show us love, and share his life. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, John 1:14: the Word became flesh. sarx is the plain word for flesh.

carryVoice: Your line: god with skin. Hunger, tiredness, thirst: the Church's claim is that God has felt them too. That's day three hundred three.

sources.q: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
which being interpreted is, God with us.
